a2z-265.description: Given an unsorted array of integers and an integer k, return the k-th smallest element. Maintain a max-heap of size k while scanning (or a min-heap of all elements), so the answer surfaces in O(n log k) time.

examples.explanation: Sorted order is 3, 4, 7, 10, 15, 20 and the third smallest is 7.

a2z-267.description: Implement a min-heap from scratch with insert(value), getMin() and extractMin() operations, each running in O(log n). Maintain the heap property with sift-up on insert and sift-down on extract, keeping the minimum at index 0 of the array.

examples.input: insert(5), insert(3), insert(8), insert(1), extractMin(), getMin()

a2z-268.description: Given an array, determine whether it represents a valid min-heap: for every index i, arr[i] must be less than or equal to arr[2i+1] and arr[2i+2] whenever those children exist. A single bottom-up check of every internal node decides it in O(n).

examples.explanation: The parent 5 is greater than its child 2.

a2z-269.description: Given an array that forms a min-heap, convert it in place into a max-heap in O(n). Run the standard bottom-up heapify (sift-down from the last internal node to the root) using the greater-than comparison instead of building it top down, which would cost O(n log n).

a2z-270.description: Given an unsorted array and an integer k, return the k-th largest element. Keep a min-heap of size k while scanning so the heap root always holds the k-th largest seen so far, finishing in O(n log k).

examples.explanation: Sorted descending the array is 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, so the second largest is 5.

a2z-271.description: Given a nearly sorted array where every element is at most k positions away from its sorted position, sort it efficiently in O(n log k) using a min-heap. Push the first k+1 elements, then repeatedly pop the minimum and push the next element.

a2z-272.description: Given k sorted linked lists (or arrays), merge them all into one sorted result. Push the head of every list into a min-heap, repeatedly extract the smallest node and push its successor, producing O(N log k) where N is the total number of nodes.

a2z-273.description: Given an array of distinct integers, replace every element with its rank: 1 for the smallest, 2 for the next, and so on. Sort a copy (or use a hashmap keyed by sorted position) and map each value to its 1-based rank.

a2z-274.description: Given a task list (uppercase letters) and a cooldown n, tasks of the same type must be separated by at least n seconds of other work or idle time. Compute the minimum total time to finish all tasks using frequency buckets or a max-heap with a cooldown queue.

examples.input: tasks = [A, A, A, B, B, B], n = 2
examples.explanation: A B idle A B idle A B fits the cooldown in 8 slots.

a2z-275.description: Given an array hand of card values and an integer groupSize, determine whether the cards can be rearranged into groups of groupSize consecutive cards. Greedily consume the smallest remaining card and its successors using a TreeMap or counters.

examples.explanation: The cards split into groups [1,2,3], [2,3,4] and [6,7,8].

a2z-276.description: Design a simplified Twitter supporting postTweet(userId, tweetId), getNewsFeed(userId) returning the 10 most recent tweets of the user and their followees, follow/unfollow, all efficiently. Keep per-user tweet lists with global timestamps and merge feeds with a heap.

examples.input: user1 posts tweets 5 then 3, user1 follows user2 who posted tweet 10, getNewsFeed(1)
examples.explanation: The feed shows tweets newest first from both the user and the followee.

a2z-277.description: Given sticks of various lengths, joining two sticks of lengths a and b costs a + b; combine all sticks into one with minimum total cost. Always join the two shortest sticks (min-heap), like Huffman merging, in O(n log n).

a2z-278.description: Design a class that receives a running stream of integers and, after each add, returns the k-th largest element seen so far. Keep a min-heap of size k so the root is always the answer, with O(log k) per addition.

examples.input: k = 3, stream starts [4, 5, 8, 2], then add(3), add(5), add(10)
examples.explanation: After adding 3 the third largest of {2,3,4,5,8} is 4, and so on.

a2z-279.description: Given two arrays a and b of equal size, a sum combination is a[i] + b[j]; return the k largest sum combinations. Start from the pair of the two largest elements in a max-heap and expand neighbours (i+1, j) and (i, j+1), avoiding duplicates with a visited set.

a2z-280.description: Design a data structure that accepts a stream of integers and returns the median of all inserted values in O(log n) per operation. Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, rebalancing so their sizes differ by at most one.

examples.output: median 5 after two adds, then 4.0, then 4.0
examples.explanation: Sorted values after all inserts are [1, 3, 5, 15] with median 4.0.

a2z-281.description: Given an integer array and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements; ties may be broken arbitrarily. Bucket values by frequency (frequency <= n) or use a heap of (count, value) pairs, achieving O(n log k) or better.

a2z-299.description: Given the root of a binary tree, produce its preorder, inorder and postorder traversals in a single pass. Use a stack of (node, state) pairs: state 1 emits preorder and pushes the node again with state 2, state 2 emits inorder and re-pushes with state 3, and state 3 emits postorder.

a2z-300.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its preorder traversal (root, left subtree, right subtree). Implement both the recursive version and the iterative stack-based version where the root is popped, recorded, and its right child pushed before its left.

a2z-301.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its inorder traversal (left subtree, root, right subtree). Implement both recursion and the iterative version: push left spine nodes onto a stack, pop, record, and move to the right child.

a2z-302.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its postorder traversal (left subtree, right subtree, root). Implement both the recursive version and the iterative versions using two stacks or a single stack with a last-visited pointer.

a2z-303.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its level order traversal: the values grouped level by level, left to right within each level. Process a queue one level at a time by snapshotting its current size, in O(n).

a2z-304.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its preorder traversal without recursion. Use an explicit stack: pop a node, record it, push its right child and then its left child so the left subtree is processed first.

a2z-305.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its inorder traversal without recursion. Use an explicit stack: descend pushing every left child, pop the deepest node, record it, and continue from its right child.

a2z-306.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its postorder traversal iteratively using two stacks. Push the root on stack 1; repeatedly pop from stack 1 into stack 2 while pushing the node's left then right children; stack 2 finally holds the postorder reversed.

a2z-307.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its postorder traversal iteratively using a single stack. Track the last visited node: while the current node exists push it and go left; otherwise peek the right child and traverse it only if it exists and was not just visited, else record the stack top.

a2z-308.description: Given the root of a binary tree, compute its preorder, inorder and postorder traversals in one traversal pass. Use a stack of (node, visitNumber) tuples and emit the node into the corresponding list on visits 1, 2 and 3, descending left then right between visits.

a2z-309.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth: the number of nodes along the longest root-to-leaf path. Compute it recursively as 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), or level-order with a counter, in O(n).

a2z-310.description: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is height-balanced: for every node the depths of its two subtrees differ by at most 1. Return the height from each recursive call (or -1 as a failure flag) so the check completes in one O(n) pass.

examples.explanation: The left subtree is two levels deeper than the right at the root.

a2z-311.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its diameter: the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes, which may not pass through the root. At each node the best path through it is leftHeight + rightHeight; track the maximum while returning heights.

a2z-312.description: Given the root of a binary tree where node values may be negative, find the maximum path sum: the largest sum of values along any path between two nodes in the tree. Each recursion returns the best gain extending downward while updating the global answer with left + node + right.

a2z-313.description: Given the roots of two binary trees, check whether they are identical: the same structure with the same values at every corresponding node. Recurse on both trees in lockstep (or compare their traversals), returning false at the first mismatch.

a2z-314.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its zigzag level order traversal: level 0 left to right, level 1 right to left, alternating each level. Process a normal level-order queue and reverse every second level (or use a deque inserting at alternating ends).

a2z-315.description: Given the root of a binary tree, print its boundary traversal: the root, then the left boundary (excluding leaves), then all leaves left to right, then the right boundary (excluding leaves) in reverse order. Handle single-node trees and children that make part of a boundary empty.

a2z-316.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its vertical order traversal: nodes grouped by vertical column (root is 0, left child -1, right child +1), columns left to right, and within a column nodes ordered by level (row, then value as tiebreak). BFS carrying (column, row) labels each node.

a2z-317.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its top view: the values visible looking down from above, i.e. the first node encountered at every horizontal distance column, ordered from leftmost column to rightmost. BFS with a column-keyed map gives the first per column.

a2z-318.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its bottom view: the last node encountered at every horizontal distance column when viewed from below, ordered left to right. BFS (or DFS with depth tiebreaks) keeping the latest node per column works in O(n).

a2z-319.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its right view: the last node of every level, i.e. the values visible from the right side. Take the final node of each level-order layer, or recurse right-first keeping the first node seen per depth.

a2z-320.description: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is symmetric around its center: the left and right subtrees are mirror images. Compare mirrored node pairs recursively (or with a queue), checking value equality and cross-wise children.

a2z-321.description: Given the root of a binary tree, print every root-to-leaf path as a sequence of node values. Recurse carrying the current path, appending each node and printing when a leaf is reached; backtracking removes the node on the way up.

a2z-322.description: Given the root of a binary tree and two nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node may be an ancestor of itself). Recurse left and right; a node whose calls return both targets is the LCA, in O(n).

examples.explanation: Both 5 and 1 hang below the root 3.

a2z-323.description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum width: the largest number of nodes present between the leftmost and rightmost non-null nodes on any level, counted with index arithmetic (children of index i are 2i and 2i+1). BFS with indices, using 64-bit arithmetic to avoid overflow.

examples.explanation: The last level spans indices 4 through 7, a width of 4.

a2z-324.description: Given the root of a binary tree, transform it so every node's value equals the sum of its children's values; you may only increase node values (never decrease), so a single root-to-leaf pass propagating children sums upward builds a valid tree in O(n).

examples.output: root becomes [150, 17, 110, 2, 15, 30, 80] style values where each parent equals its children's sum

a2z-325.description: Given the root of a binary tree, a target node and an integer k, return all node values at distance exactly k from the target, where edges connect a node to its parent and children. Build a parent map with one traversal, then BFS outward k levels from the target.

examples.explanation: 7 and 4 lie two edges below 5, and 1 is two edges above via the root.

a2z-326.description: Given the root of a binary tree and a start node value, a fire starting there spreads to adjacent nodes every second; compute the minimum time to burn the entire tree. Map each node to its neighbours (including parents) and BFS level by level from the start.

examples.explanation: At t=1 nodes 1, 4, 5 catch fire and at t=2 the last node 3 does.

a2z-327.description: Given the root of a complete binary tree, count its nodes in less than O(n) time. Compare the leftmost and rightmost spine heights: if equal the subtree has 2^h - 1 nodes, otherwise recurse on both halves, giving O(log^2 n).

a2z-328.description: State the combinations of traversals that uniquely reconstruct a binary tree: inorder plus any one of preorder, postorder or level order is sufficient, while preorder with postorder alone leaves ambiguous trees. Explain why inorder's split property pins down the root's position.

a2z-329.description: Given the preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree (values distinct), construct the tree. The first preorder element is the root; its inorder index splits left and right subtrees; recurse on the two halves using an index map for O(n).

a2z-330.description: Given the postorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree (values distinct), construct the tree. The last postorder element is the root; its inorder index splits the subtrees; recurse right subtree first because postorder lists it before the left, using an index map for O(n).

a2z-331.description: Design serialization: convert a binary tree to a string (for example preorder with null markers) and deserialize it back into the identical tree. Any format works as long as encode and decode are inverses; a queue consuming tokens rebuilds the tree in O(n).

examples.output: serialize(root) = '1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#', and deserialize returns the original tree

a2z-332.description: Given the root of a binary tree, perform preorder traversal in O(n) time and O(1) extra space using Morris threading. Temporarily link each node's rightmost left-subtree descendant back to the node, follow the thread after the left subtree finishes, and remove the temporary link.

a2z-333.description: Given the root of a binary tree, perform inorder traversal in O(n) time and O(1) extra space using Morris threading. Before descending left, find the predecessor (rightmost node of the left subtree) and thread it to the current node; when the thread is found again, record the current node and cut the thread.

a2z-334.description: Given the root of a binary tree, flatten it into a 'linked list' in place: the list uses the right pointers only and follows preorder order, with every left pointer null. Reverse-think recursively (flatten right then left, relinking a global tail) or use Morris-style re-linking.
